short_title: Kilusan ng Mamamayan para sa Matuwid na Bayan v. COMELEC
full_title: KILUSAN NG MAMAMAYAN PARA SA MATUWID NA BAYAN, A COALITION OF CORPORATE ENTITIES DULY REGISTERED WITH THE SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION, WHICH ARE PETITIONERS HEREIN AS WELL, NAMELY, CAPITOL CHRISTIAN LEADERSHIP; BUKLOD PAMILYA INCORPORATED; KMP, KOALISYONG PANGKAUNLARAN NG MAMAMAYAN; AND KNK, ANAK NG DIYOS KADUGO NI KRISTO, AND JOSE LAGUNSAD GONZALES, VICENTE ALEJO MACATANGAY, JR., SHARON FAITH SAMACO PAQUIZ, NELSON JAVA CELIS, MELCHOR GRUELA MAGDAMO, RODRIGO G. CORNEJO, AND MELANIO LAZO MAURICIO, JR., PETITIONERS, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS (COMELEC), RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: V. Special Civil Actions > E. Certiorari, Prohibition, and Mandamus (Rule 65)
topics: Verification and certification against forum shopping in a Rule 65 petition (Rule 7, Secs. 4-5)
Proof of service on the adverse party (Rule 56, Sec. 2(c); Rule 13, Sec. 17)
Competent evidence of identity must appear on the face of the notarized verification or affidavit
Petitioners who do not sign the verification and certification are dropped
Legal standing of organizations and of citizens asserting a public right

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VI. Judicial Department > B. Judicial Review > 1. Requisites

doctrine:
A petition for mandamus filed with the Supreme Court must carry proof of service on the adverse party (Rule 56, Sec. 2(c), in relation to Rule 13, Sec. 17) and a proper verification and certification against forum shopping (Rule 65 in relation to Rule 7, Secs. 4 and 5). The affiant's competent evidence of identity must appear in the notarized verification and the affidavit of service (2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, Rule II, Secs. 2, 6 and 12). **Parties who did not execute the verification and certification, including organizations with no authorized representative, are dropped as petitioners. Where the remaining petitioners still fail to cure the defects after the Court ordered compliance, the petition is dismissed.** ID copies attached at the end of the compliance do not cure a verification whose face does not show the affiants' competent evidence of identity. That the IDs were shown to the notary is "a mere speculation."

On standing (reiterated, AES Watch v. COMELEC): organizations that allege only that they are juridical entities able to sue, that their boards authorized the suit, and that their members face public scrutiny for their advocacy **do not show the personal and substantial interest required for legal standing**. Individuals suing as citizens without alleging material injury may be given relaxed treatment when the proceeding asserts a public right (Francisco v. House of Representatives). Here, however, the procedural dismissal made relaxation pointless.

Mandamus to compel the COMELEC to issue implementing rules will not issue where petitioners fail to substantiate their claim that no such rules exist. The Court noted that COMELEC resolutions already govern the matters raised. It also reiterated that a PCOS machine's signature may be the equivalent of a digital signature (Capalla; Bagumbayan-VNP).
facts:
Kilusan ng Mamamayan para sa Matuwid na Bayan (KMMB), a coalition of SEC-registered entities, four of its member organizations, and seven individuals filed a petition for mandamus against the COMELEC. They asked the Court to compel the COMELEC to promulgate implementing rules under the Omnibus Election Code and RA Nos. 7166, 8436 (as amended by RA 9369) and related laws. They also asked that the COMELEC first hold public consultations on, among others: the minimum system capabilities under Section 7 of RA 9369; the right of watchers and the public to take photographs; electronic digital signatures of Board members; transmission of election returns to the KBP; and a truly random manual audit. They invoked Section 9, Chapter 2, Book VII of the Administrative Code of 1987 on public participation in rule-making. They said the COMELEC committed grave abuse of discretion by not acting on KMMB's February 14, 2022 letter. They also prayed for a TRO stopping the COMELEC from using Smartmatic machines for the 2022 elections and after until the rules were issued.

Petitioners targeted specific COMELEC issuances. These were Resolution No. 8786, Section 40(f) and (g) (instructing BEIs to press "NO" when the PCOS asks whether to digitally sign transmission files), Resolution No. 10458, Section 4 (timing of the random selection of precincts for the random manual audit), and the ban on capturing devices "for whatever purpose" inside the polling place.

In a Resolution dated April 19, 2022, the Court required petitioners to submit proof of service of the petition on the COMELEC, a proper verification and certification against forum shopping (the affiant lacked competent evidence of identity), and competent evidence of identity of the affiant in the affidavit of service. In their Compliance, petitioners submitted Mauricio, Jr.'s affidavit that he served the petition by e-mail to the COMELEC's public address, but the notarial page did not show his competent evidence of identity. The new verification and certification, executed by Macatangay, Jr., Paquiz, and Gonzales, lacked Paquiz's signature. No competent evidence of identity appeared below the affiants' names, although copies of IDs of Macatangay, Jr. and Gonzales were attached as the last pages. Two member organizations had no authorized representatives and no one verified for them. Petitioners Celis, Magdamo, Cornejo, and Mauricio, Jr. never executed a verification and certification.
issues: Whether the petition should be dismissed for petitioners' failure to cure the defects in the proof of service and in the verification and certification against forum shopping.
Whether petitioners have legal standing to file the petition.
Whether petitioners substantiated their claim that the COMELEC failed to issue implementing rules for the safeguards of automated elections.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the petition is dismissed on procedural grounds.** The affidavit of service did not show the affiant's competent evidence of identity. The verification and certification lacked Paquiz's signature, and the affiants' competent evidence of identity did not appear below their names. That the IDs attached at the end of the Compliance were shown to the notary at notarization was "a mere speculation as the competent evidence of identity... do not appear on the face of the Verification and Sworn Certification Against Forum Shopping." **The two organizations without authorized representatives, and Paquiz, Celis, Magdamo, Cornejo, and Mauricio, Jr., who did not execute a verification and certification, were dropped as petitioners.** The remaining petitioners, "despite being given the chance to rectify the procedural infirmities," failed to correct them, so the petition was dismissed.

**2. The organizations lack standing; the individual citizens might have been allowed relaxed standing, but this was rendered unnecessary.** Standing asks whether a party has alleged "such a personal stake in the outcome of the controversy as to assure that concrete adverseness" that sharpens the issues (AES Watch). The organizations alleged only juridical capacity, board authorization, and public scrutiny of their members. **These averments did not meet the requisite personal and substantial interest.** The remaining individual petitioners, Macatangay, Jr. and Gonzales, alleged no material injury. A relaxation would have been warranted since they sued as citizens, and under Francisco v. House of Representatives, "when the proceeding involves the assertion of a public right, the mere fact that he is a citizen satisfies the requirement of personal interest." But the petition was already dismissible on procedural grounds.

**3. No.** Petitioners failed to substantiate their claim that there are no implementing rules for the safeguards under Section 7 of RA 9369. Their own petition cited the random manual audit and Resolution No. 10088, among other COMELEC resolutions, as measures governing automated elections. In AES Watch, the Court had noted that Resolution No. 10460 for the 2019 elections already removed the phrase "for whatever purpose" from the ban on capturing devices. The ban now targets devices used to copy the contents of the ballot or identify one's vote. AES Watch also reiterated Capalla v. COMELEC that PCOS machines are capable of digitally signed transmissions. Citing Capalla, Bagumbayan-VNP Movement, Inc. v. COMELEC found no infirmity in treating a PCOS machine's signature as the equivalent of a digital signature.
disposition: The Petition for Mandamus was DISMISSED, and the prayer for a temporary restraining order and/or any injunctive relief was DENIED.

bar_questions.q: Ten petitioners, consisting of three non-stock corporations and seven individuals, filed with the Supreme Court a petition for mandamus against a government agency. The verification and certification against forum shopping was signed by only two individuals, and the notarial jurat did not state any competent evidence of identity. The Court ordered petitioners to submit proof of service and a proper verification and certification. In their compliance, the same two individuals executed a new verification, again without competent evidence of identity indicated in the jurat, but they attached photocopies of their IDs at the last pages. No one signed for the corporations or for the five other individuals. What should the Court do with the petition?

alac.answer: The Court should drop as petitioners the corporations and the five individuals who did not execute the verification and certification, and dismiss the petition as to the rest for failure to cure the procedural defects.
alac.legal_basis: A petition under Rule 65 must be verified and carry a certification against forum shopping (Rule 65 in relation to Rule 7, Secs. 4 and 5). It must be accompanied by proof of service on the adverse party (Rule 56, Sec. 2(c), in relation to Rule 13, Sec. 17). The affiant's competent evidence of identity must appear in the notarial certificate (2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, Rule II, Secs. 2, 6 and 12). Parties who did not execute the verification and certification, including organizations with no authorized representative, are dropped as petitioners. When the remaining petitioners fail to correct the defects despite being given the chance, the petition is dismissed (Kilusan ng Mamamayan para sa Matuwid na Bayan v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 259850, June 13, 2023).
alac.application: The three corporations had no authorized representative who executed a verification and certification, and five individuals never executed one. They must be dropped. The two who signed were already directed to cure the defect but again submitted a jurat without competent evidence of identity on its face. Photocopies of IDs at the end of the compliance do not show that those IDs were presented to the notary; that is mere speculation. Having been given the opportunity and having failed to use it, the remaining petitioners cannot expect further leniency.
alac.conclusion: The non-signing parties are dropped and the petition is dismissed for uncured procedural defects.

bar_questions.q: A coalition of civic organizations filed a petition questioning a COMELEC resolution on automated election safeguards. It alleged only that its members are juridical entities with capacity to sue, that their boards authorized the suit, and that their leaders face public scrutiny for their advocacy. Two individual voters joined the petition. They alleged no personal injury but claimed to sue as citizens to enforce the public's right to clean elections. (a) Do the organizations have legal standing? (b) May the individual petitioners be given standing?

alac.answer: (a) No, the organizations lack legal standing. (b) Yes, the rule on standing may be relaxed for the individuals because they sue as citizens asserting a public right, provided the petition is otherwise procedurally sound.
alac.legal_basis: Standing requires that a party allege such a personal stake in the outcome of the controversy as to assure concrete adverseness (AES Watch v. COMELEC). In Kilusan ng Mamamayan para sa Matuwid na Bayan v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 259850, June 13, 2023), the Court held that allegations of juridical capacity, board authorization, and public scrutiny of members do not meet the requisite personal and substantial interest. For citizens, when the proceeding involves the assertion of a public right, the mere fact of citizenship satisfies the requirement of personal interest (Francisco v. House of Representatives, applied in Kilusan, supra).
alac.application: (a) The coalition's allegations show capacity to sue and authority to file, but no direct injury or personal and substantial interest in the COMELEC resolution. These are the same averments found insufficient in Kilusan. (b) The two voters allege no material injury, but they sue as citizens to enforce a public right connected with the integrity of elections. In Kilusan, the Court said such relaxation "would have been warranted" for similarly situated citizens. It did not apply it only because the petition was dismissed on procedural grounds.
alac.conclusion: The organizations have no standing, while the citizen-petitioners may be accorded relaxed standing if the petition is otherwise in order.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Santos, a notary public, notarized the verification and certification against forum shopping of a petition filed in the Supreme Court. The jurat states that the affiants "personally appeared and exhibited their government-issued IDs," but it does not identify any ID or its details. The affiants are not personally known to Atty. Santos. (a) Is the jurat compliant with the Rules on Notarial Practice? (b) What is the effect on the petition if the defect is not cured after the Court orders compliance?

alac.answer: (a) No. The jurat does not show the affiants' competent evidence of identity. (b) The petition may be dismissed for failure to cure the defective verification and certification.
alac.legal_basis: Under the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, Rule II, Sections 2, 6 and 12, the affiant in a jurat must personally appear before the notary and, if not personally known to the notary, be identified through competent evidence of identity. In Kilusan ng Mamamayan para sa Matuwid na Bayan v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 259850, June 13, 2023), the Court required that the competent evidence of identity appear on the face of the verification and certification and of the affidavit of service. It dismissed the Rule 65 petition when petitioners failed to cure this and other defects despite an order to comply.
alac.application: (a) The affiants were not personally known to Atty. Santos, so their identity had to be established through competent evidence of identity, which the jurat should reflect. A general statement that unspecified IDs were exhibited does not show on the face of the document what evidence of identity was presented. (b) A verification and certification so notarized is defective. If the petitioners do not correct it after the Court gives them the chance, the petition may be dismissed, as in Kilusan.
alac.conclusion: The jurat is defective, and an uncured defect of this kind may cause the dismissal of the petition.

notes: Leonen, Acting C.J. wrote a separate concurring opinion. It discussed the mandatory nature of the AES minimum capabilities, the COMELEC Advisory Council, and the mootness of the 2010 and 2019 issues; none of this is examinable. The main opinion does not decide whether Section 9, Chapter 2, Book VII of the Administrative Code (public participation) binds COMELEC rule-making, or the elements of mandamus. Footnote 2 notes that the first page captioned the petition as one for certiorari, mandamus and prohibition, but the Court treated it as a petition for mandamus. Footnote 26 notes that petitioners misquoted Section 20 of Resolution No. 10460. Q3(a) applies the general notarial rule on jurats as cited (Rule II, Secs. 2, 6 and 12); the decision does not quote those provisions.
